transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-09
Time: 15:00 - 15:58 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jared Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Tomas Vega (Redwood SE), Maya Liu (Cottonwood Head of ML), Ethan Shaw (Cottonwood Platform Eng), Lori Bennett (Procurement), Samir Rao (SRE)

Summary (auto):
Redwood walked Cottonwood through the Optimize console playbook for session forecasting, prefetched KV/prefix caching recommendations, and an initial cost model. Key topics: sessionization patterns, TTL defaults, cache warmup strategies, batching/concurrency trade-offs, hosted vs dedicated routing, and security/KMS concerns. Agreed next steps: share cost spreadsheet, provide sample traces, run sandbox benchmark.

Topics:
- Session forecasting and heatmaps
- KV / prefix cache design (TTL, eviction, lookahead)
- Batching and concurrency settings impact on unit cost
- Fallbacks: hosted/dedicated model variants and region routing
- Security and compliance (SOC 2, KMS, VPC)

Action items (brief): see metadata list above

Transcript:
[00:00] Jared (Redwood AE): All right, everyone good to start? I think we have about an hour. Thanks for making time. 
[00:05] Maya (Cottonwood): Yep, good to go. Sorry, running a little late earlier.
[00:08] Priya (Redwood SE): No problem. Today we'll focus on session forecasting and then dig into KV / prefix cache choices that map to the cost model Tomas prepared. We'll demo the Optimize console briefly and run through a couple of simulations.
[00:18] Ethan (Cottonwood): Quick ask — we care a lot about tail latency under load and also keeping cost below our current infra bill for inference. So the tradeoffs matter.
[00:22] Jared: Totally. We'll show numbers — synthetic but based on similar fintech workloads — and then we'll plug in your trace.
[00:29] Tomas (Redwood SE): One note up front: when we say KV cache, sometimes the transcription or docs call it K V cash, so just ignore those typos. It's the same prefix/KV cache we use to store token-level past keys for session re-use.

[00:45] Priya: Okay starting with session forecasting. Can you describe how long sessions are and what a "session" means for you? Are sessions user sessions or chat sessions persisted across days?
[00:52] Maya: For us, a session is user conversation state that persists for up to 24 hours. Typical interaction is 4-6 turns, but we get bursts during market open where a subset of power users will run 20+ turns in short windows.
[01:10] Samir: And we pin certain users for low-latency routing; those are our fast-path.
[01:14] Priya: Perfect. That variability — 4–6 mostly but spikes to 20+ — is exactly where prefix caching and lookahead prefetch can save tokens and cost. Our playbook usually recommends a TTL around the median session length and a longer TTL for pinned users, with a warmup/pre-fetch window for expected spikes.
[01:33] Ethan: How do you choose the TTL? If we set it too long we'll waste memory and if too short we'll cold-start and lose savings.
[01:38] Priya: Right. We pick TTL by looking at the session heatmap: percentiles of session length. For example, if 75th percentile is 10 turns, TTL at 12 turns captures most reuse. Then for power users you might pin a 60–90 min TTL. We'll also use a small LRU eviction slab for non-pinned sessions.
[02:00] Tomas: In the Optimize cost model spreadsheet we included three scenarios: conservative (short TTL), balanced (median TTL + small prefetch), and aggressive (long TTL + lookahead). The cost delta can be 15–45% between conservative and aggressive depending on hit rate and prefetch efficiency.

[02:18] Maya: Those deltas sound big. Can you show the sim for market-open spike patterns?
[02:22] Priya: Yep, switch to the Optimize console. (link in chat: https://redwood.app/optimize/demo-ct-playbook) There is a heatmap widget — you can upload traces or use our sample noise model.
[02:31] [screen share noise — chatter]
[02:40] Priya: Here I've loaded a sample trace that emulates your morning spike; note the session density per minute. See how lookahead prefetch improves batch sizes by ~1.7x and reduces per-token GPU time by applying KV reuse earlier.
[02:57] Ethan: Wait when you say lookahead prefetch — is that speculative generation of keys beyond the current prompt?
[03:03] Priya: Good point — it's not speculative generation of tokens. It's pre-warming the KV cache for a model variant using predicted next-turn tokens footprint — basically if you know a user is likely to do a short follow-up you pre-attach the KV prefix so the runtime doesn't need to re-compute from scratch. It's driven by sequence length heuristics, not hallucinated content.
[03:24] Maya: And prefetch costs money, right? If you pre-warm for lots of sessions you'll pay for the compute.
[03:28] Tomas: Exactly. That's why the cost model includes a prefetch inefficiency penalty: prefetch cost - avoided compute. If your follow-up probability is >0.6 and the average saved tokens > X then prefetch pays off.

[03:44] [05:00 marker — brief mute for connection noise]
[05:12] Jared: Another lever is batching and concurrency. Small-ish batches keep latency down but increase cost; larger batches increase throughput but may push tail latency. Priya will show batching curves.
[05:23] Priya: Here's our batching sensitivity chart. For a 4k context LLM on A100ish hardware we see sweet spots. In your case with many short sessions, continuous batching with a 50–150ms window and concurrency cap of 8 keeps p99 under target while improving tokens/sec.
[05:45] Ethan: Can Redwood enforce session affinity to keep cache hits on same worker? We want consistent hit rates.
[05:52] Priya: Yes, session affinity is supported — you can shard by session ID and we keep warm KV fragments on the same worker. There are tradeoffs: affinity reduces cross-worker batching effectiveness, so we balance affinity pins for hot sessions only.

[06:10] Samir: For security, we need to ensure KV data is encrypted and doesn't leave our VPC. How does the private deployment model handle that?
[06:18] Tomas: For Private deployments (VPC/on-prem), the control plane still orchestrates but customer-managed networking keeps inference inside your VPC. KV cache memory is ephemeral on the GPU nodes and can be configured to use envelope encryption with your KMS/HSM. We'll share our SOC2 + KMS integration doc.
[06:32] Lori: Procurement question — what's the delta between hosted and dedicated pricing for heavy prefetch workloads?
[06:38] Jared: Hosted is usage-based; heavy constant prefetching will show on per-token compute line items. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and cost per reserved capacity; if your peak usage justifies it, dedicated ends up cheaper at scale. We'll include both scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[06:52] Maya: Can Redwood route to a cheaper model variant during non-market hours automatically?
[06:56] Priya: Yes, our smart routing can use time-of-day, latency SLO, and cost policies to route to smaller/quantized variants at night. We also support automatic fallbacks if capacity constrained.

[07:10] Ethan: About the cache eviction — how do we avoid long-tail growth if a user accumulates many ephemeral sessions?
[07:16] Priya: We recommend per-customer quota + LRU with TTL enforcement. The quota is based on expected concurrent session count times average warmed KV footprint. If quota is hit, oldest non-pinned sessions are evicted. We also support periodic recompact to free GPU memory for burst windows.

[07:35] [07:40 timestamp — slight audio skip]
[07:46] Tomas: I'll point out one modeling caveat: quantization impacts per-token latency differently across models. Our spreadsheet flags models where 4-bit quantization gives big CPU/GPU kernel speedups vs ones where attention kernels are bottlenecked. For some of your workload patterns, a quantized variant + prefix cache is actually the best cost path.
[08:05] Maya: Ok show me a conservative vs aggressive row for our morning spike example.
[08:10] Priya: Conservative: TTL 6 turns, no lookahead prefetch, small batching windows -> baseline cost X. Balanced: TTL 12 turns plus prefetch on high-probability sessions -> cost -17%. Aggressive: TTL 30 turns + prefetch + pin 5% of users -> cost -33% but memory use up 2.8x.
[08:36] Ethan: Those memory numbers worry me. If memory goes up 2.8x we might need more nodes. How does Redwood compute the node count?
[08:42] Tomas: Node count is a function of total warmed KV memory + model footprint + desired headroom. The console's capacity estimator shows recommended node counts per scenario. We'll simulate with your traces and you can pick autoscaling/burst options.

[09:00] Maya: How intrusive is instrumentation? We can't send PII.
[09:03] Priya: We only need anonymized session traces: timestamps, session IDs (hashed or ephemeral), turn lengths, and some flags for pinned users. No message contents.
[09:12] Ethan: We'll scrub and provide that.

[09:20] [10:00 marker — short pause]
[10:12] Jared: Let's walk through an example path — user A makes three short requests and then a 15-turn burst at market open. We'll show how lookahead prefetch plus pinning switches the session to pinned fast-path.
[10:25] Priya: (walkthrough) First two short requests hit small-batch path, we don't prefetch. Third request sees pattern and triggers prefetch policy because probability of follow-up >0.7; we warm the KV and increment session hotness score. When burst arrives, the session is pinned and remains on worker node with big-KV slab.
[10:47] Ethan: Nicely dynamic. Does pinning keep the session pinned after prolonged inactivity?
[10:51] Priya: No, pinning TTL decays; default is 30 min, configurable. We also have manual admin APIs to pin/unpin programmatically.

[11:00] Tomas: I'll show the console capacity planner now — model, warmed KV bytes per session, concurrency, headroom, recommended nodes.
[11:09] [screen share showing table — low res alt text: capacity table rows] 
[11:18] Priya: See row for 'balanced' — recommended 4 nodes with 20% headroom, expected p95 latency 220ms and price estimate $0.078 per 1k tokens (synthetic).
[11:30] Maya: That $0.078/1k tokens — how do you calculate it? Does it include prefetch wasted tokens?
[11:35] Tomas: It includes GPU cost (amortized), idle overhead, and prefetch penalty. We annotate each line with assumptions. You can toggle whether prefetch is charged fully or amortized over expected hits.

[11:50] Samir: About metrics and observability — can we get token-level traces and per-session costs in the console?
[11:57] Priya: Yes, the Console has token-level cost breakdown and a per-session dashboard. We'll show a sample later.

[12:08] Lori: Procurement: do you offer committed reserved pricing for Dedicated?
[12:12] Jared: Yes, Dedicated has reserved capacity contracts monthly/annual and we can add burst capacity. We'll include an illustrative committed vs on-demand cost line in the sheet.

[12:25] Ethan: If we want to start with hosted but move to dedicated later, is config portable?
[12:30] Priya: Absolutely — same API and rollout policies. You can pin model variants and routing policies and flip the deployment behind the scenes. That's a Redwood differentiator.

[12:42] Maya: Any gotchas about cache warmup periods when migrating?
[12:46] Tomas: Just expect initial cold-starts; we recommend a seeding phase where you preload the most active sessions or run a short synthetic replay to warm KVs.

[13:00] [13:10 marker — background noise as someone types]
[13:18] Priya: Quick note on eviction policies: besides LRU we support frequency-based and cost-aware eviction where we evict low-value sessions that cost more to keep than they'd save. This ties directly to the cost-model's per-session ROI column.

[13:34] Maya: Could you walk through the ROI calc quickly?
[13:38] Tomas: Sure. ROI = (expected compute saved by hit-rate * token-cost) - (prefetch cost + memory opportunity cost). We compute memory cost as marginal node cost divided by warmed bytes capacity; it's an approximation but useful for relative comparisons.

[14:00] Ethan: Can we plug in our AWS pricing or on-prem cost model?
[14:03] Priya: Yes, the spreadsheet accepts custom hardware dollars per-hour and you can set region multipliers. We'll send the template.

[14:12] Maya: If we set too many pins, does the autoscaler respect reservation?
[14:16] Tomas: Autoscaler uses configured headroom and will spin extra nodes if required, but pinned session memory is taken into account. For Dedicated, you can configure a hard node cap.

[14:30] [15:00 marker — quick Q/A pause]
[15:05] Ethan: A question on function/tool calling — we use some external tools in flows. Does prefetch break tool calling correctness?
[15:11] Priya: No, tool calling stays deterministic; prefetch is only about KV/state reuse. If you use dynamic tools that depend on external state, we don't prefetch tool outputs.
[15:20] Maya: Good. Also we need audit logs of who accessed sessions.
[15:24] Tomas: Audit logs are available — token-level traces are scrubbed but access logs include session IDs (hashed) and user/context metadata. We'll share the log retention options.
[15:35] [16:00 marker — connection hiccup briefly] 
[16:10] Jared: Wrapping to practical next steps: we need sample traces, we'll run the sandbox sim, return with actual predicted node count and cost delta.
[16:20] Maya: We'll prepare the traces. One ask — can you annotate which prefetch policies are safe for compliance? 
[16:26] Priya: Yes, in the policy template we flag policies that act only on metadata (turn counts, probability) vs ones that would need content inspection. We'll send the template.
[16:36] Ethan: About SSO and SAML for Console access?
[16:39] Tomas: Full SSO/SAML and RBAC supported; can be integrated with your IdP.
[16:44] Lori: Any standard SLA for Dedicated?
[16:47] Jared: Yes, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs depending on tier — we'll include those in the enterprise packet.
[16:56] Maya: Great. When can we run the benchmark? The week of Sep 20 works.
[17:00] Jared: We'll aim for Sep 21 for the 1-hour run. Tomas will own it.
[17:06] Tomas: Yep I'll set up the sandbox and share instructions today.
[17:10] Priya: I'll also mark recommended TTL defaults and eviction policy in a short note.
[17:14] Jared: Anything else on cost model assumptions?
[17:17] Ethan: Just want clarity on how prefetch expenses are amortized.
[17:20] Tomas: We'll include an amortization toggle and show both full-charge and amortized views.
[17:25] [18:00 marker — people looking at spreadsheet] 
[18:10] Maya: Ok thanks, this was helpful. We like the session affinity and the dynamic pin idea.
[18:16] Jared: Good. Final recap: Redwood sends cost model + SOC2/KMS doc, Cottonwood provides anonymized traces, Redwood runs 1-hour sandbox benchmark week of Sep 20, follow up call to review results.
[18:30] Lori: Procurement will review dedicated pricing.
[18:33] Samir: We'll include SRE concerns in the shared doc.
[18:37] Jared: Thanks everyone. We'll email meeting notes and links in the next 24 hours.
[18:43] Maya: Thanks all. Bye.
[18:46] End meeting.
